spec.title: One spine, many profiles, an honest crosswalk
spec.intro:
Your team is consolidating five framework obligations onto one internal spine. Your
workspace holds exactly what `bash setup.sh ./work` stages on a real machine: the
twenty valid 800-53 family abbreviations (`work/spine-families.txt`) and a seed
crosswalk with four rows — one of them a deliberately planted orphan. The "Run
validator" button runs the same logic as the lab's `validate-crosswalk.ts`, ported and
verified byte-for-byte in CI against real runs of the committed validator, always
against whatever your crosswalk says RIGHT NOW — its verdicts are earned, never
scripted. Where the module's lab redirects output into `validation-before.txt` and
`validation-after.txt`, you copy the verdict into those files here; same artifact,
same discipline. One familiar face: the seed's `SC-28` row is the data-at-rest claim —
the laptop-encryption question you have been asking machines since module 00 — now
seen from the MODEL stage, where one encrypted-disk evidence package gets to answer
four frameworks at once. One honesty note: the validator checks structure (real
families, no orphans, legal labels). Whether a label tells the truth is yours to
supply — the lab makes you feel exactly where that line sits.

tasks.instruction:
§6 task 1 — orientation. Open `work/spine-families.txt` and `work/crosswalk.csv`
and read them. Then write one sentence each: what the spine file IS (what those
twenty two-letter rows are, and what they are FOR in this table), and what a
crosswalk row IS (its four columns and what a single row claims).

hints.nudge: The spine file is the answer to: which values may a row's spine_control start with? Count its lines. The crosswalk's header names the row's anatomy.

hints.concept: §4.1 — families as the addressing scheme; §4.6 — the crosswalk row

tasks.instruction:
§6 task 2 — add three rows to `work/crosswalk.csv` mapping these requirements to
spine controls: SOC 2 `CC7.2` (system monitoring), ISO 27001 `A.8.15` (logging),
and CIS v8 `8.2` (collect audit logs). All three concern logging/monitoring —
decide which of the twenty families they belong to, pick a control number in it,
and give each row an HONEST relationship label (`exact` / `broader` / `narrower` /
`partial`). Mind the shapes: a broad outcome criterion is rarely `exact` against
one control, and a prescriptive safeguard is usually the narrow end of its line.

hints.nudge: Logging and monitoring have a family of their own — say its full name, then its two letters. For labels: re-read each row aloud as a claim about how much of the requirement that one control covers.

hints.concept: §4.4–4.6 — what kind of object each framework is decides which end of the line is narrow

hints.reveal: Append: SOC2,CC7.2,AU-6,narrower · ISO27001,A.8.15,AU-2,exact · CIS8,8.2,AU-2,narrower — AU is Audit and Accountability; CC7.2 is a broad criterion one AU control only partly answers, and CIS 8.2 is a prescriptive safeguard.

tasks.explain:
Three frameworks, three dialects, one family — that convergence is the load-bearing
fact of the whole module, and you just recorded it as data. Notice what the labels
bought you: `exact` only where the meanings genuinely line up, `narrower` where a
single control answers only a slice. A reviewer can now read coverage off the
table instead of taking your word for it.

tasks.instruction:
§6 task 3 — find the planted orphan row in the seed (its `spine_control` is
empty). Do NOT delete it and do not fix it yet. In one or two sentences: name the
spine control it SHOULD map to (the module names the likely home — a system
component inventory control), and explain why papering over it with a
loosely-related control instead would be a false equivalence.

hints.nudge: PCI's 6.3.2 wants an inventory of bespoke and custom software. Which family manages configurations and components? What does mapping it to, say, an access-control row silently claim?

hints.concept: §4.7 + §5.3 — an orphan is a signal, not a clerical error; force-fitting converts an honest gap into a hidden over-claim

tasks.instruction:
§6 task 4 — run the validator UNRESOLVED: press **Run validator** with the orphan
still in place. Confirm the verdict: exit code `1`, and the orphan named by
profile and control. Then capture the verdict: copy the full output (summary
line, FAIL lines, and the `exit: 1` line) into `validation-before.txt`, replacing
its placeholder — the in-browser stand-in for
`bun validate-crosswalk.ts work/crosswalk.csv > validation-before.txt 2>&1`.

hints.nudge: Nothing to fix yet — the point of this run is to watch the machine refuse. A check that cannot fail verifies nothing; keep the refusal as evidence.

hints.concept: §5.4 — the validator's verdict, the way a machine reports it; §4.4 of module 01 — exit code as the verdict

hints.reveal: Press Run validator (it exits 1, naming PCI4 6.3.2), then select validation-before.txt and paste the output: the profiles/rows summary line, the two FAIL lines, and exit: 1.

tasks.explain:
That exit code is a machine-readable verdict a CI gate can act on — no human
reading required to know the crosswalk isn't yet trustworthy. And the capture you
just kept is evidence in the audit sense: when someone asks "how do you know the
orphan was caught before it was resolved?", `validation-before.txt` IS the answer.

tasks.instruction:
§6 task 5 — resolve the orphan: edit the `PCI4,6.3.2` row, fill in the correct
`spine_control` (`CM-8`, system component inventory) and an honest non-`orphan`
relationship label. Press **Run validator** again and confirm it now exits `0`.
Capture the passing verdict into `validation-after.txt`, replacing its
placeholder — copy the output exactly as the validator printed it.

verify.stdout_matches: PASS: every profile requirement maps to a real spine family

hints.nudge: Change only the orphan row: spine_control becomes CM-8, relationship becomes the honest call (does CM-8 cover the requirement and more, or only part of it?). If the validator still exits 1, its output names exactly what's left.

hints.concept: §5.3 — the orphan's job is to be resolved deliberately: extend the spine, or correct the mapping

hints.reveal: Rewrite the row as PCI4,6.3.2,CM-8,broader · press Run validator (profiles: 5 | rows: 7 | spine families referenced: 4/20, then the PASS line) · paste those two lines into validation-after.txt.

tasks.explain:
The fail-then-pass pair you now hold is the artifact pattern this whole curriculum
keeps producing: a check that refused, the deliberate fix, and the same check
blessing the result. The crosswalk stopped being a spreadsheet someone asserts is
complete and became a VERIFIED artifact — the exact table module 12 converts to
OSCAL without a rewrite.

tasks.instruction:
§6 task 6, part one — a deliberate false equivalence. Take the seed's data-at-rest
row (`CSF2,PR.DS-01,SC-28,partial` — the crosswalk face of the laptop-encryption
claim) and temporarily relabel it `exact`. Press **Run validator** and read its
verdict carefully. Read the row aloud as a claim: "encryption-at-rest alone fully
satisfies the data-at-rest outcome."

hints.nudge: Yes, really — make the dishonest edit. The lesson only lands when you watch what the machine does with it.

hints.concept: §4.7 — the validator enforces vocabulary, not truth; false equivalences look complete

hints.reveal: Change the row's last cell from partial to exact and press Run validator: it still exits 0. exact is in the allowed set — the machine cannot know it's a lie.

tasks.explain:
The validator said PASS — and that is the most important verdict in this lab,
because it is wrong about the one thing it cannot see. Structure was legal;
semantics were false. §5.2 already showed you why: PR.DS-01 takes SC-28 AND key
management AND validated crypto together. This is the exact boundary §4.7 drew —
machines catch structure, completeness, and vocabulary; the honesty of a label is
forced into the open precisely so a HUMAN must make the call you just unmade.

tasks.instruction:
§6 task 6, part two — in one sentence, state why the `exact` claim you just made
is false for this row: what else does the data-at-rest outcome require that
encryption-at-rest alone does not provide? (The laptop-encryption thread gives you
the concrete version: the disk is encrypted — what about the keys, and the
algorithm's strength?)

hints.nudge: §5.2 maps PR.DS-01 to a SET of three spine controls, each honestly partial. Name what the other two cover.

hints.concept: §5.2 — a one-to-many map where every line labeled exact would be a lie

tasks.instruction:
§6 task 6, part three — restore the honest label: set the `CSF2,PR.DS-01,SC-28`
row back to `partial` and run the validator once more, leaving the crosswalk
validator-clean with every label telling the truth again.

hints.nudge: Same cell, honest value. The validator's verdict won't change — which is the point you just proved — but the table's truthfulness does.

hints.concept: §4.6 — the relationship column is the honesty call, not decoration

hints.reveal: Change exact back to partial on the CSF2 row and press Run validator (exit 0).

tasks.explain:
Note what changed and what didn't: the machine's verdict is identical before and
after, but the table now tells the truth. That delta — invisible to the validator,
decisive to an auditor — is why §4.7 says the artifact is DESIGNED to force the
human judgment into the open rather than pretend a machine can make it.

tasks.instruction:
§6 task 7 — write the crosswalk's `README.md` (replace the placeholder) in 4–6
sentences, for a teammate who has never seen the table: what the spine is; why
800-53 is the spine and not one of the profiles (the superset argument — use the
word); how to read a row's relationship label (name all four); and what the
validator guarantees versus what it deliberately cannot (who supplies the
semantic honesty).

hints.nudge: Four required ideas, one or two sentences each: spine, superset, the four labels, the machine/human split. You lived all four in the last six tasks — write what happened.

hints.concept: §3 — the whole model in one sentence; §4.7 — what machines catch and what they can't

hints.reveal: Cover, in order: (1) the spine is the one catalog we own, (2) 800-53 is the superset so smaller frameworks map onto it downhill, (3) exact/broader/narrower/partial say how much of the requirement the spine control covers, (4) the validator guarantees structure — real families, no orphans, legal labels — while semantic honesty is supplied by a human.

tasks.explain:
That README is the difference between a table you understand and a table the TEAM
owns. Notice it documents the validator's limits as carefully as its guarantees —
writing down what a check cannot catch is the same discipline as keeping
validation-before.txt: it makes the boundary auditable instead of assumed.

tasks.instruction:
The defense, in writing (4–6 sentences), for a colleague who has only ever worked
inside one framework: walk them out of the trap. Start where §3 starts — what
happens to a program that builds one control set per framework — then explain the
way out using the spine-and-profile model in your own words, and end with what the
four frameworks you touched today (SOC 2, ISO 27001, CSF 2.0, CIS v8) each ARE,
in one honest phrase apiece.

hints.nudge: The trap is structural, not personal: five control sets, 70% the same control said five ways, drifting apart. The way out is one sentence — frameworks become views onto a single source of truth you own.

hints.concept: §3 — the mental model; §4.2–4.5 — what kind of object each framework actually is
